newsitem.title: CHINA: China interbank volume shrinks on stock crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China interbank volume shrinks on stock crackdown.

text.p: China's local currency interbank market saw its trading volume shrink dramatically over the past six weeks after a government crackdown on the stock market slashed demand for funds, analysts said on Wednesday.

Average daily turnover on the Shanghai-based market has fallen to around 1.5 billion yuan ($181 million) since the start of July, compared with 2.3 billion yuan in the first half of 1997, and 2.7 billion yuan in 1996, official figures showed.
"The plunge is due to the recent measures to standardise the financial markets," an interbank market trader said.
"The most important factor has been steps to enforce a ban on securities firms using money they borrow on the interbank market to trade on the stock market," he said.
Securities firms are confined to trading on the market's second tier, which is conducted through short-term financial centres or money brokerages run by the central bank.
Securities firms must borrow money for not more than one day and use the funds only to balance their accounts.

The financial centres and state-owned banks trade on the first tier, which allows them to use the exchange's computerised trading system to borrow and lend money directly among themselves for terms of up to 120 days.
In May, China cracked down on stock market speculation, triggering a downturn on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses and curtailing the business of securities firms.
"Securities houses are major borrowers on the (interbank) market, and the reduction of their business has caused the demand for funds to decrease sharply," another interbank trader said.
"This has caused an oversupply of funds on the (interbank) market and depressed daily turnover," he said.

Volume of first-tier trading exceeded second-tier trading in July for the first time since the interbank market was launched in January 1996, following the cutback in borrowing by securities houses, dealers said.
The interbank market was originally envisioned as the key barometer of short-term money supply in China. But recent falling volume showed that goal was still far away, analysts said.

Persistent rumours that Beijing would cut bank reserve ratios also contributed to the fall in interbank volume as market players were unwilling to build long-term positions due to uncertainty over the move, analysts said.
A cut in the 13 percent ratio -- the sum Chinese banks must deposit with the central bank as a proportion of total deposits -- would release more funds and limit demand on the interbank market.
The People's Bank of China, the central bank, has declined to comment on rumours of a possible cut.
Analysts said banks have found it cheaper to acquire funds on the interbank state debt market and this has also caused turnover to fall on the yuan interbank market.
Turnover on the local currency interbank market was not expected to recover in the short term, dealers said.
"The crackdown on the financial markets has not been met with corresponding measures to support activity," said an official with a major Chinese state bank.
"And measures (to support activity) won't be worked out in a short period."
